newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major tries to bind party's wounds on Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major tries to bind party's wounds on Europe.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major cracked the whip on Tuesday over his feuding ministers to try to halt a new bout of infighting over Europe that is threatening to tear the ruling Conservative party apart.

Major intervened hours after junior Foreign Office minister Sir Nicholas Bonsor whipped up party passions to fever pitch by accusing finance minister Kenneth Clarke of stepping out of line with the government in comments on European monetary union.

Soon after the Treasury was forced to deny rumours in financial markets that Clarke had resigned, Major's office issued a statement saying both ministers fully supported the government's agreed policy on a single currency.
"The prime minister has made it clear that all ministers must adhere fully to the position agreed in cabinet," the statement, a thinly veiled rebuke to both men, said.

Major was said to be furious with Clarke for declaring on Sunday in his typically robust manner that it would be "pathetic" for Britain to wait and see how a European single currency developed before deciding whether to join.
The government's official policy, which Major crafted to try to bridge the yawning divide between pro-Europeans and so-called Eurosceptics in his party, is to keep all options open.

Euro-sceptics, who have been pressing Major to rule out joining the single currency during the five-year term of the next parliament, to be elected by May, were incensed that Clarke had expressed such overt support for a single currency.
Although some rank-and-file Conservatives called for Clarke to resign, political commentators were astonished that Bonsor should attack a much more senior colleague in public.

"I think he will be out of line with the view of the vast majority of the party and I think it is out of line with what the government policy has been as expressed before," Bonsor, who makes no secret of his Euro-sceptic views, told BBC radio.

"I think the difference between Mr Clarke and some of us is that he thinks we can have a single European currency without having a federal Europe. We think...that would be an inevitable step down a road we don't want to advance down," he added.
Major's office later said that Bonsor had given his interview based on press reports of what Clarke, the cabinet's leading pro-European, had said and now accepted he was mistaken.
"He fully supports the government's position," a spokesman for the prime minister said.
He said Clarke, too, who was en route to a meeting of Commonwealth finance ministers in Bermuda, also "fully supports the policy and believes his views have been misrepresented".

The latest squabbling -- extraordinary even by the standards of the Conservatives' long-running civil war on Europe -- bodes ill for Major's hopes of presenting a united front at the party's showpiece annual conference in two weeks' time.
The opposition Labour Party, 20 points ahead in opinion polls, said Bonsor had smashed the principle of collective government and brought the party's splits into the open.

"With such division and disunity now the dominant feature of this government, ministers are no longer fit or able to represent British interests in Europe or elsewhere," Gordon Brown, Labour's economics spokesman, said in a statement.
